name: Bosnia-Herzegovina

narrative.essence: Bosnia-Herzegovina returns to the World Cup for only the second time — a nation that has existed for barely 30 years, born from one of Europe's most devastating conflicts. Their qualification is a sporting miracle wrapped in a story of resilience that goes far beyond football.
narrative.footballIdentity: Football in Bosnia is identity made visible. Three main ethnic communities — Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats — found something rare under the Zmajevi crest: a shared team to support. The 2014 World Cup qualification was a breakthrough; the team was filled with European league talent led by Edin Džeko. Now a new generation carries that tradition forward. For many Bosnians, national football is the only thing that crosses ethnic lines.
narrative.theMoment: Bosnia qualifies with a squad built around Bundesliga and Serie A talent, a generation raised in the shadow of the 2014 breakthrough. The country's political structure — the Dayton Agreement that created separate governing entities — still makes governing football complicated. Manager Sergej Barbarez, a Bosnian legend who played in Germany, is trying to create something more unified than the country's political reality. The sport is ahead of the politics.

keyPlayers.name: Ermedin Demirović
keyPlayers.note: The clinical finishing machine who scored prolifically in the Bundesliga. Bosnia's most dangerous forward and the focal point of everything they build.

keyPlayers.name: Sead Kolašinac
keyPlayers.note: Physical, relentless fullback who provides width and energy. His attacking presence down the left is a consistent asset.

keyPlayers.name: Amir Hadžiahmetović
keyPlayers.note: Engine of Bosnia's midfield. High work rate, good range of passing, and defensive discipline that holds the structure together.

keyPlayers.name: Amar Dedić
keyPlayers.role: Dynamic attacking full-back who overlaps relentlessly and contributes heavily going forward

tactics.tacticalNote: Bosnia play a direct 4-3-3 that leverages physicality and set-piece quality. Demirović's movement pulls defenders while Kolašinac bombs forward from left-back. Pjanić's delivery from dead balls is their biggest weapon in any game situation. They're well-drilled, hard to bully, and capable of punishing the slightest defensive lapse.
tactics.strength: Set pieces and physicality — Bosnia is dangerous at every dead ball and can bully teams who aren't prepared for their physicality.
tactics.vulnerability: Against top teams, they concede too much space between midfield and defense — they're caught too high up the pitch when the press fails.

watchFor: Pjanić's set-piece deliveries — corner and free kick routines are carefully rehearsed and Demirović is an excellent aerial target.
Kolašinac overlapping on the left — when Bosnia wins the ball centrally, the first option is often to play wide left and let him run.
Bosnia's reaction to falling behind — their directness increases when chasing games, which can be a strength or create more space to counter.
